title: Ang 137–145: Majh ki Var
hook: Guru Nanak's ballad in Majh, first half
tomorrow: what would a mosque built out of mercy look like?

segments.voice: Yesterday, your month: twelve months, twelve questions, and in Kattak, good deeds and no blaming anyone else. Now another ballad.

A package lands on your porch with your street on it and a stranger's name. A cashier hands back a twenty when you paid with a ten. A paycheck has a few extra hours you never worked. Nobody would ever know. So what's the one thing that's never yours to take? Guru Nanak's Majh ki Var, which opens on ang 137, has a line for exactly this, and it speaks to two neighbors at once.
screen: `A STRANGER'S PACKAGE.` → `A TWENTY FOR A TEN.` → `NOBODY WOULD KNOW.`

segments.voice: Majh ki Var is Guru Nanak's ballad in Majh, built like the first var, saloks set before pauris. Its very first salok, on ang 137, praises the Guru, in paraphrase: the Guru is the giver, the Guru is a house of cool snow, the Guru is the lamp of the three worlds. Cool, when everything's heating up. A few pages on, ang 141, comes a line about money and what isn't yours. In paraphrase: to take what is rightfully another's, Nanak says, is pork to the Muslim and beef to the Hindu. He reaches each neighbor with their own deepest line, the food they'd never touch, and lays it over taking what isn't yours. Then he keeps going, in paraphrase: the Guru and the guide will stand by you only if you don't eat what's dead. Talk alone won't get you to heaven; you're freed by living the truth. Truth, lived, from ang 62, again. So what does this give you for a week like this one? A bright line, not a debate. Not, is it really stealing if they made the mistake. Just: is it rightfully mine? If not, it's off the plate, whoever's watching or not.
screen: `THE GURU, A HOUSE OF COOL SNOW.` · `ANOTHER'S DUE: OFF THE PLATE.` · `TALK WON'T GET YOU THERE.` · `IS IT RIGHTFULLY MINE?` · then, large: `THE MAJH BALLAD.`

segments.voice: If you can, read one salok of Majh ki Var first. Then look around for one thing near you that isn't yours: a borrowed charger, a sibling's hoodie, a library book, a neighbor's container. Set it by the door, or wherever its owner will find it, and sit the rest of the time with your hands open and empty.
Ang 137. The page where Guru Nanak's Majh ki Var begins, with the Guru as a house of cool snow.
Your line for today: the majh ballad, and its bright line, what's another's is never yours. Go easy.
